opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is this: if we want a model to act autonomously, to go out into the world, do long tasks, interact with people and environments, then most of the signal it gets back won't be a clean scalar reward. In reinforcement learning today, especially the RL that made reasoning models work, we rely heavily on verifiable rewards. Did you get the math answer right? Did the code pass the unit tests? That's one bit, maybe a few bits, of information per episode. It works remarkably well in domains where you can build a verifier, but it's extremely low-bandwidth, and most of the real world doesn't come with a verifier.

Think about how humans actually learn on the job. When you start working somewhere, nobody gives you a reward of 0.7. Your colleague says, "This analysis is fine, but you misunderstood what the client cares about," or "Next time check the logs before you restart the service." That's natural language, and it carries far more information than a scalar. It tells you *what* went wrong, *why*, and often *how* to fix it. A person can take one sentence of feedback and change their behavior right away, across many future situations. Current models mostly can't do that in a durable way. You can put the feedback in the context window and the model will follow it for that conversation, but it doesn't really get absorbed into the model. Once the context is gone, the lesson is gone.

So I see two gaps. The first is sample efficiency. If learning depends only on outcome rewards, you need enormous numbers of trials to work out credit assignment, which steps were good and which were bad. Language feedback can, in principle, do much of that credit assignment for you. The second is open-endedness. An autonomous agent will keep running into tasks nobody designed a reward function for. The one universal interface for telling it what we want, and what it did wrong, is language. If the model can't learn efficiently from that, then every new capability requires humans to engineer a new reward or a new dataset, and that isn't autonomy. That's just us doing the learning on the model's behalf.

That's why I call it foundational rather than one more technique. It sits beneath a lot of things people want: continual learning, personalization, agents that improve while deployed. All of them come down to the same question: can the model turn experience plus a critique into a lasting change in its own behavior? We have pieces of it. Reflection, in-context learning, and distilling corrected trajectories back into the weights all help. But we don't yet have a clean, general, scalable recipe the way we do for next-token prediction or for RL with verifiable rewards. I think whoever gets that right opens up the next stage, where models stop being trained once and then frozen and instead keep learning from the people and the world they work with.

r001.rationale: The response says scalar rewards carry very little information, while language feedback explains what went wrong, why, and how to fix it, conveying the loss of dimension-specific guidance in a scalar.

r002.rationale: It says outcome-only learning requires enormous numbers of trials to determine which steps were good or bad, matching inefficient inference of the criteria from repeated rewards.

r003.rationale: It identifies language feedback as a way to provide credit assignment and corrective guidance, and says an autonomous agent must learn efficiently from it to improve its behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that for a long time the whole field has been training models on signals that are far too thin compared to the actual richness of what we know.

Think about how a person learns a skill. When you make a mistake, nobody hands you a single number, a zero or a one. Someone tells you, in words, what went wrong, why it went wrong, and often what you should try next time. That sentence carries an enormous amount of information. It tells you which part of your behavior was the problem, it tells you the direction to move in, and it often gives you the underlying principle so you can generalize to cases you have never seen. A scalar reward gives you none of that. It tells you that something was off, and then the model has to spend a huge number of samples discovering what.

So from a pure efficiency standpoint, if you have a channel that can carry orders of magnitude more information per episode, and you are not using it, you are leaving most of the signal on the table. That alone would make it important.

But I think the deeper reason is about autonomy itself. If you want a model to operate for long stretches without a human in the loop, it has to be able to improve from whatever the environment gives back. In the real world, that feedback is almost never a clean reward. It is a user saying "that's not quite what I meant," a compiler error, a reviewer leaving comments, a colleague pushing back. All of that is language. A system that can only learn from numeric rewards is dependent on someone else translating the world into numbers for it, and that someone is a human. So it is not really autonomous. It is still tethered.

There is also a verification angle that I find quite important. When a model learns from a reward, the lesson it extracts is opaque. You see the behavior change but you cannot read the reason. When a model learns from language, the lesson is at least in principle legible. You can look at the feedback it received, you can look at how it updated, and you can judge whether the update was reasonable. For systems we intend to trust with more and more responsibility, that legibility is not a nice-to-have.

And the last piece, which I think people underestimate, is that natural-language feedback is the only kind of signal that scales with the complexity of the task. For simple tasks, a reward is fine, because the space of ways to be wrong is small. For open-ended tasks, the space of failure modes explodes, and the only thing expressive enough to point at a specific failure in that space is language. So as we push models toward harder, longer-horizon work, I think this stops being an optimization and starts being a requirement. That is why I call it foundational rather than just useful.

r001.rationale: The response explains that language identifies which part of behavior failed and how to improve, while a scalar reward gives none of that dimension-specific information.

r002.rationale: It says a model given only a scalar reward must spend many samples discovering what went wrong.

r003.rationale: It connects autonomy to learning from real-world environmental feedback, which it describes as language, and explains that such feedback gives a direction for improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s foundational because an autonomous model needs to improve from the consequences of its actions. You can train a model before deployment, but you can’t anticipate every situation it will encounter or every preference a user will have. So the question is: when someone tells it what went wrong, can it use that feedback to do better next time?

Natural language is a rich way to provide that signal. A person can say, “Your answer is technically correct, but you made an assumption that doesn’t apply here.” That tells the model much more than a thumbs-down. But it also creates a difficult learning problem: the model has to interpret the feedback, identify which decision it refers to, and figure out how broadly the correction should apply.

And responding correctly in that moment isn’t enough. If the model apologizes and then repeats the same mistake on a slightly different task, it hasn’t really learned. We need that feedback to produce a lasting improvement, without making the model blindly accept every correction or forget things it already knows. That ability to turn interaction into reliable learning is, to me, a core requirement for autonomy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses natural-language feedback as a rich signal, but does not say that reducing multidimensional evaluations to one scalar reward loses dimension-specific feedback.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a model inferring scoring criteria from scalar rewards through repeated sampling.

r003.rationale: The response says a model should interpret feedback and use it to improve, but does not identify extracting improvement directions from natural-language interactions with the environment as a prerequisite for autonomous learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s foundational because an autonomous model needs to keep learning after we deploy it. We can’t anticipate every situation during training, and we can’t expect people to provide a perfectly specified reward function for every task. What people naturally provide is language: “You misunderstood my goal,” “This part is useful, but you missed a constraint,” or “Try approaching it this way.”

That feedback contains much richer information than a simple success or failure signal. But the model has to figure out what the feedback means, which decision it applies to, and how to use it in future situations. Sometimes it should update its understanding of the task; sometimes it should change its strategy; sometimes it needs to ask a clarifying question.

So the core problem is turning communication into reliable improvement. If a model can do that, a person can guide it without having to reprogram or retrain it for every new situation. That’s a basic capability we need for systems that can operate autonomously while remaining responsive to human intent.

r001.rationale: The response says language feedback is richer than a success-or-failure signal, but does not state that reducing multidimensional evaluations to a scalar loses dimension-specific feedback.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that a model given only scalar rewards must infer the scoring criteria through repeated sampling.

r003.rationale: The response says autonomous models need to interpret natural-language feedback, identify how to improve or change strategy, and use it for reliable improvement and continued learning.
